Draft:

More Than One Voice

Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide whether to take a job in another city. She asked her mother, who told her to stay close to home. If Dana had stopped there, she would have turned the job down. Instead she kept asking, and what she heard from four different people changed her mind twice before she finally settled on an answer she trusted. Watching her go through that taught me why asking several people for advice usually leads to a better decision than asking just one.

The first reason is that every person who gives advice sees only part of the picture. Dana's mother thought about how lonely a new city can be, because she had moved once herself and hated it. Dana's old manager thought about the salary and the title, because that is what he knows. A friend who already lived in that city talked about rent, traffic, and how long it took her to make friends there. None of them was wrong, but none of them had the whole story either. When Dana put their answers side by side, she had something closer to a complete map. One adviser gives you one angle. Several give you the corners you could not see from where you were standing.

A second reason is that people have their own interests, even when they love you. Dana's mother wanted her nearby. That is a kind thing to want, but it is not the same as wanting what is best for Dana's career. In the same way, a salesperson who tells you which phone to buy may be honest, but he also earns a commission. If you ask only him, you cannot tell where his advice ends and his interest begins. If you also ask a friend who owns the phone and read what a repair technician says about it, the bias of any one source gets diluted. When three people with different stakes all say the same thing, you can trust it more than you could trust any one of them alone.

Third, disagreement is useful. When two people Dana respected gave her opposite answers, she had to figure out why. It turned out that her manager assumed she wanted to move up quickly, while her friend assumed she cared most about having free time. Their disagreement pointed to a question Dana had not asked herself: what did she actually want out of the next five years? Doctors understand this, which is why patients facing surgery are often encouraged to get a second opinion. If the second doctor agrees, the patient goes in with more confidence. If the second doctor disagrees, the patient has learned that the decision is not as simple as it first sounded, and that is worth knowing before anyone picks up a scalpel.

Of course, asking more people has limits. Ten opinions can leave a person more confused than two, and at some point collecting advice becomes a way to avoid deciding. The answer is not to count votes. Dana did not take the job because three out of four people told her to. She took it because the conversations showed her what mattered to her and what the real risks were, and then she chose for herself.

Seeking multiple opinions does not hand the decision to a crowd. It gives the person deciding better material to work with: more facts, a check on any one adviser's bias, and questions that would not have come up otherwise. Dana has been in her new city for eight months now, and she still calls her mother every Sunday.
